report:
### Conclusion
The claim that taking ibuprofen for COVID-19 worsens the infection is **unsupported by scientific evidence**. Clinical studies and health organizations confirm that ibuprofen and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) do not increase COVID-19 severity, hospitalization, or mortality.

### Origins of the Concern
In March 2020, French Health Minister Olivier Véran cautioned against using ibuprofen, suggesting anti-inflammatories might aggravate COVID-19 infections (https://www.wired.com/story/the-ibuprofen-debate-reveals-the-danger-of-covid-19-rumors/). This view stemmed from early theoretical hypotheses that NSAIDs could upregulate ACE2 receptors—the entry mechanism for SARS-CoV-2—or suppress fever, potentially dampening the initial immune response.

### Clinical Evidence & Health Consensus
Subsequent research comprehensively investigated these concerns and found no harm:

- **Public Health Statements:** The World Health Organization (WHO) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued guidance stating there is no scientific evidence linking ibuprofen to worsening COVID-19 symptoms or disease progression (https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/ibuprofen-covid-19-novel-coronavirus-1.5501496, https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-advises-patients-use-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs-nsaids-covid-19).
- **Meta-Analytic Data:** Systematic reviews pooling observational and clinical data across thousands of patients demonstrated that NSAID exposure is not associated with higher mortality, ICU admission, or severe clinical outcomes in COVID-19 patients (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34339037/).

### Summary
While patients should always adhere to recommended dosages and consult healthcare providers, current evidence shows ibuprofen can be safely used to manage pain and fever during a COVID-19 infection.
